Conventional wisdom is any idea, belief, or explanation that most people in a society accept as true — not necessarily because it has been proven beyond doubt, but simply because it has been widely repeated, rarely challenged, and passed down over time.
Breaking Down the Two Words

To really understand the term, it helps to look at the two words separately.

"Conventional" means something that follows convention — that is, the usual, accepted, or standard way of thinking or doing things in a group or society. It's what the majority agrees on without much argument. "Conventional" often implies something old, comfortable, and unquestioned.

"Wisdom" normally means deep, reliable knowledge and good judgment gained from experience or reflection. True wisdom is usually accurate and trustworthy.

Now, here's the interesting tension: when you put these two words together, the phrase does not actually guarantee truth. "Conventional wisdom" is wisdom in name, but it is only conventional in practice — meaning it is popular and widely believed, not necessarily verified or correct.
The Core Idea, Explained Simply

Imagine that almost everyone in your neighborhood believes that drinking cold water when you have a cold will make it worse. Nobody has really studied this. Nobody proved it. But parents told children, children told friends, and friends told strangers — and eventually, nearly everyone just accepted it as true. Nobody questions it anymore because everybody believes it.

That shared, unquestioned belief — that is conventional wisdom.

It is the default answer that most people reach for when asked about a topic, without feeling the need to double-check it.
Where the Term Comes From

The phrase "conventional wisdom" was made famous by the American economist John Kenneth Galbraith in his 1958 book The Affluent Society. He used it — quite critically — to describe ideas that are accepted not because they are accurate, but because they are familiar, comfortable, and safe.

Galbraith noticed that people in politics, economics, and everyday life tend to prefer ideas that do not disturb or challenge the status quo. These comfortable, familiar ideas become the "conventional wisdom" of their time — and they can be very hard to dislodge, even when new evidence contradicts them.
How Conventional Wisdom Forms

Conventional wisdom does not appear overnight. It builds up gradually through a predictable pattern:

Step 1 — Someone says something. An idea is introduced — sometimes by an expert, sometimes by a popular figure, and sometimes just by a random person who spoke loudly and confidently.

Step 2 — It spreads. People repeat the idea to others. It appears in books, articles, speeches, casual conversations.

Step 3 — It becomes "common knowledge." After being repeated enough times, the idea stops being questioned. It enters the background of daily life as something "everyone knows."

Step 4 — It becomes invisible. The idea is now so embedded in society that people forget how it started or whether anyone ever proved it. It is simply assumed to be true. Questioning it starts to feel strange or even rude.

At this point, it has become conventional wisdom.
A Key Characteristic: It Feels Obvious

One of the most important features of conventional wisdom is that it feels obvious to the people who hold it. They don't feel like they're believing something on faith — they feel like they're just stating plain common sense.

This is what makes conventional wisdom so powerful and also so potentially dangerous. When an idea feels obvious, people stop examining it. And when people stop examining something, errors can survive for a very long time.
Examples That Make It Clear

Here are some examples of things that have been (or still are) conventional wisdom at various points in history:

Example 1 — The Earth is flat.
For most of human history, this was the default belief of ordinary people. It felt obvious — you can look around and the ground looks flat. Sailors, travelers, and common folk simply accepted it. It was conventional wisdom, not science.

Example 2 — You should eat three meals a day.
This is widely accepted as healthy fact. But in reality, historians note this pattern was largely shaped by industrial work schedules and social customs in the 19th century — not by nutritional science. It is largely conventional wisdom, not a universal biological law.

Example 3 — Ulcers are caused by stress.
For decades, the medical world accepted this as settled fact. Doctors told patients to reduce stress and change their diets. Then in 1984, two Australian scientists (Barry Marshall and Robin Warren) discovered that most ulcers are actually caused by a bacterium called Helicobacter pylori. They were initially laughed at — because they were challenging conventional wisdom. They later won a Nobel Prize.

Example 4 — Blood should be kept in the body during surgery.
For most of medical history, bloodletting — draining blood from sick patients — was considered effective treatment. Physicians across the world practiced it confidently. It was wrong, and it killed people. But for centuries, it was conventional wisdom.

Example 5 — A college degree always leads to success.
This is a widespread belief in many modern societies. It may have been more reliably true in certain decades, but in many contexts today it is an oversimplification. Still, it circulates widely as if it were an absolute truth.
When Conventional Wisdom Is Right

It would be unfair and inaccurate to say conventional wisdom is always wrong. Sometimes, a widely-held belief is widely held because it is correct. Through repeated experience, societies often stumble onto useful truths that get passed down correctly.

For example:

  • "Wash your hands before eating" — was common wisdom long before germ theory explained why it worked.
  • "Don't drink seawater when you're thirsty at sea" — sailors knew this from experience before the science of osmosis was understood.
  • "Exercise is good for your health" — broadly true, and also broadly believed.

The point is not that conventional wisdom is always false. The point is that it is not reliable proof of truth by itself. You cannot say something is true just because "everyone knows it." The validity of a belief must be checked independently.
When Conventional Wisdom Is Dangerous

Conventional wisdom becomes dangerous when:

It discourages questioning. Because the idea is "what everyone knows," raising doubts can feel socially awkward or even rebellious. This social pressure protects wrong ideas from scrutiny.

It is used to justify important decisions. When policymakers, doctors, or business leaders make major choices based on unexamined conventional wisdom, the consequences can be serious.

It serves someone's interests. Sometimes, a belief becomes "conventional wisdom" because powerful people — corporations, governments, institutions — benefit from promoting it. The idea that cigarettes were harmless was, for a time, nearly conventional wisdom in parts of society — a view that the tobacco industry spent enormous money to create and sustain.

It is mistaken for expert consensus. People often confuse conventional wisdom (popular opinion) with scientific consensus (carefully studied expert agreement). These are very different things. Scientific consensus changes slowly and is based on evidence. Conventional wisdom can change fast and is based on popularity.
Conventional Wisdom vs. Scientific Consensus

This distinction is important enough to deserve its own section.

Conventional wisdom is what most ordinary people believe. It is shaped by culture, media, repetition, and social norms. It requires no formal study or evidence.

Scientific consensus is what a large body of qualified researchers agree on after careful, repeated, peer-reviewed study. It is also not perfect — science evolves — but it is far more reliable than popular belief.

For example, that human activity is causing climate change is scientific consensus. That "we only use 10% of our brains" is conventional wisdom — and it is false.

Always be careful not to use these two concepts interchangeably.
How to Think About Conventional Wisdom in Real Life

Here is a simple mental framework you can use whenever you hear something that sounds like conventional wisdom:

Ask: "How do we know this?"
Is the belief based on careful study, or is it just something that has been repeated a lot?

Ask: "Who benefits from this belief being widespread?"
Sometimes beliefs spread because they serve the interests of powerful people or institutions.

Ask: "Has anyone checked this recently?"
Some ideas were true in one era but are outdated in another. Circumstances change.

Ask: "What is the actual evidence?"
This is the most important question. Evidence is the difference between knowledge and assumption.
A One-Paragraph Summary to Remember

Conventional wisdom is the body of ideas, beliefs, and assumptions that most people in a society accept without much questioning — not because they have been proven rigorously, but because they have been repeated so widely and for so long that they feel like obvious common sense. The term was popularized by economist John Kenneth Galbraith to describe beliefs that are comfortable and familiar, rather than necessarily correct. Conventional wisdom can sometimes be right, but it can also preserve serious errors for generations. The key insight is this: widespread belief is not the same as truth. Something being "what everybody knows" is not evidence that it is accurate — it is only evidence that it is popular. The critical thinker treats conventional wisdom as a starting point for inquiry, not as the end of it.
